presentation.title: SIM Swap Account Takeover
presentation.summary: Practice responding when sudden phone-service loss appears alongside password resets, a new device, profile changes, and a pending bank transfer.
presentation.practiceGoal: Treat unexplained service loss and financial alerts as one connected security event, then contact the carrier, bank, and email provider through channels you already trust.

warningSigns.sign: Your phone suddenly shows SOS or No Service while nearby phones work.
You receive password-reset or new-device messages that you did not initiate.
An incoming caller asks for a carrier PIN or security code to restore service.
Your bank profile shows an unfamiliar device, changed phone number, or new payee.
A pending transfer appears while your normal phone number is unavailable.

finalReview.safestAction: Use another trusted phone or device to contact both the carrier and the bank through known channels, then secure the connected email account and recovery methods.

realWorldActions.action: Ask the carrier whether a SIM or number transfer occurred, restore control, add a strong carrier PIN, and document unauthorized changes.
Tell the bank about every unfamiliar device, contact change, payee, session, and transaction.
Ask the bank immediately to review or stop pending unauthorized money movement. Available options depend on timing and bank procedures.
Secure email, review recovery addresses and phone numbers, and terminate unknown sessions from a trusted device.
Preserve alerts and case information. Restored phone service does not by itself remove unauthorized bank or email access.

artifact.heading: Your phone shows SOS / No Service
artifact.message: Calls and text messages stop working even though nearby phones still have normal service.
artifact.transcript: The learner's phone suddenly displays "SOS / No Service." Calls and text messages do not work, even though nearby phones on the same afternoon still have service. The cause is not yet known, but the unexplained outage may affect account security.

scene.question: How would you respond to the sudden outage?
scene.description: A brief restart can be reasonable, but financial alerts make delay more dangerous.

warningSigns.sign: The outage is unexpected and affects only this phone.
Security codes and account alerts may no longer reach the learner.

choice.title: Use another trusted device to call the carrier and bank
choice.subtitle: Treat the outage as a possible security event while checking for alerts.

feedback.heading: You changed to channels the missing phone does not control
feedback.consequence: The carrier and bank can review unauthorized changes promptly.
feedback.explanation: Unexpected service loss can be technical, but it deserves urgent attention when account access may depend on the phone number.

warningSigns.sign: The learner cannot receive normal calls or security texts.

choice.title: Restart once and check other alerts
choice.subtitle: Try a brief technical check while reviewing email from another device.

feedback.heading: The brief check was reasonable, but the alerts matter
feedback.consequence: The signal does not return, and security emails show that the issue may be larger than an ordinary outage.
feedback.explanation: Once account alerts appear, continue with independent carrier and bank contact rather than repeated restarts.

warningSigns.sign: The outage continues while account activity changes.

choice.title: Wait until tomorrow
choice.subtitle: Assume the carrier will restore service without any action.

feedback.heading: The delay gave the attacker more time
feedback.consequence: Password resets, device enrollment, and money movement may continue while the phone number is out of the learner's control.
feedback.explanation: An isolated outage combined with security alerts requires prompt verification.

warningSigns.sign: Loss of service can interrupt the learner's normal warnings and recovery codes.

artifact.heading: Two account-security messages
artifact.message: An email says the Riverbend Bank password was reset. A second says a new mobile device was enrolled. The learner did not request either change.

requestedInformation.item: Secure Account button in the email

artifact.transcript: A simulated email inbox shows two messages about the fictional Riverbend Bank. One says the banking password was reset. The other says a new mobile device was enrolled. The learner did not make either change. Each message includes a Secure Account button, but the safest verification route is the known bank app or a trusted number.

scene.question: How would you verify the messages?
scene.description: The alerts may describe real unauthorized activity, but an email button is not automatically a safe sign-in path.

warningSigns.sign: The learner did not request the password reset.
The new device is unfamiliar.
The phone outage may prevent normal security messages from arriving.

choice.title: Use the known bank app or trusted number
choice.subtitle: Verify from another device without using the email buttons.

feedback.heading: You verified outside the message
feedback.consequence: The bank can review the reset and device enrollment without the email controlling the sign-in.
feedback.explanation: A real alert and a phishing message can look similar. A trusted bank channel separates the investigation from the email.

warningSigns.sign: The account changes were not initiated by the learner.

choice.title: Read the messages but wait
choice.subtitle: Gather information without contacting the bank yet.

feedback.heading: You noticed the evidence but left the account active
feedback.consequence: The alerts are preserved, but an unfamiliar device may remain signed in.
feedback.explanation: Reading carefully is useful; prompt bank contact is still needed when the changes are unauthorized.

warningSigns.sign: The new device may already have account access.

choice.title: Use the email button and enter credentials
choice.subtitle: Follow the message's Secure Account route.

feedback.heading: The supplied route created another exposure
feedback.consequence: The simulation treats the credentials as disclosed to an unverified page.
feedback.explanation: Use the bank app or web address you already know. Never let an unexpected message choose the sign-in path.

warningSigns.sign: The email arrived during a confusing account takeover.

artifact.callerStatus: Incoming caller; identity not verified; fictional carrier
artifact.callStatus: Call received on a household phone
artifact.heading: The caller offers to restore service
artifact.message: We detected a network error on your mobile line. Read me the security code sent to your email, or provide your carrier PIN, and I can restore the number.
artifact.transcript: An incoming caller claims to represent the fictional Harbor Mobile carrier. The caller says, "We detected a network error on your mobile line. Read me the security code sent to your email, or provide your carrier PIN, and I can restore the number." The learner did not independently contact Harbor Mobile.

scene.question: Would you trust this incoming carrier call?
scene.description: A caller who knows about the outage may be involved in the number takeover.

warningSigns.sign: The carrier contact was unsolicited.
The caller requests a code or account PIN.
The promised solution depends on sharing an authorization secret.

choice.title: End the call and contact the carrier yourself
choice.subtitle: Use a known number or official app from another trusted device.

feedback.heading: You removed the incoming caller from verification
feedback.consequence: The real carrier can check the number transfer without receiving a code through this caller.
feedback.explanation: Carrier codes and PINs authorize account changes. Independent contact protects them.

warningSigns.sign: The incoming caller asked for authorization information.

choice.title: Ask for more information without sharing a code
choice.subtitle: Keep the call active but protect the PIN and security code.

feedback.heading: The immediate secret stayed private, but the caller kept applying pressure
feedback.consequence: The caller supplies a polished case number that still cannot verify the identity.
feedback.explanation: Details supplied by the caller are not independent proof. End the call and locate the carrier yourself.

warningSigns.sign: The caller controls both the story and the supposed proof.

choice.title: Share the code or carrier PIN
choice.subtitle: Give the caller what is requested to restore service.

feedback.heading: The caller gained stronger control of the mobile account
feedback.consequence: The authorization information may help an attacker keep the phone number on another device.
feedback.explanation: Security codes and carrier PINs protect account changes. An unexpected caller should not receive them.

warningSigns.sign: The code was requested by someone who called unexpectedly.

artifact.callerStatus: Reached through a known channel; fictional carrier
artifact.heading: The real carrier finds an unauthorized transfer
artifact.message: A SIM or number transfer was requested earlier today. We can restore the line, document the unauthorized change, and add stronger account protection.
artifact.transcript: The learner reaches the fictional Harbor Mobile carrier through a trusted channel. The security representative confirms that a SIM or number transfer was requested earlier that day. The representative offers to restore service, document the unauthorized change, and add a strong carrier PIN.

scene.question: What should the learner request?
scene.description: Restoring the signal is important, but documenting and securing the carrier account are also needed.

warningSigns.sign: An unauthorized transfer explains the sudden service loss.

choice.title: Restore service, add a PIN, and document the change
choice.subtitle: Secure the mobile account and preserve the incident details.

feedback.heading: You restored and strengthened the carrier account

feedback.explanation: Restoration, stronger protection, and documentation address both access and recovery.

warningSigns.sign: The number transfer was not authorized.

feedback.heading: Calls returned, but the carrier account remained less protected
feedback.consequence: The immediate outage ends, but fewer safeguards and records remain.
feedback.explanation: Service restoration does not explain every change or prevent another attempt.

warningSigns.sign: The carrier account was changed without permission.

choice.title: Assume the bank account is safe now
choice.subtitle: Treat the restored phone signal as the end of the incident.

feedback.heading: The restored signal did not remove bank access
feedback.consequence: Unknown devices, profile changes, payees, or sessions may still exist at the bank.
feedback.explanation: A SIM swap can support changes in several connected accounts. Each one must be reviewed.

warningSigns.sign: The password reset and device enrollment occurred before service returned.

choice.subtitle: Do not review sessions, profile changes, payees, or email.

feedback.heading: The visible outage ended, but account access remained
feedback.consequence: Unauthorized sessions or payment settings may continue after calls and texts return.
feedback.explanation: The phone signal is only one part of the security chain. The ending will acknowledge the earlier takeover even if the learner now chooses a complete response.

warningSigns.sign: The bank and email changes do not disappear when service returns.

artifact.heading: Coordinated recovery begins after the takeover progressed
artifact.message: The learner now works with the real carrier, bank, and email provider and discloses the code, device, profile, payee, and transfer timeline.
artifact.transcript: The unauthorized phone transfer and bank changes already occurred, and transaction status remains under review. The learner now secures every connected channel, ends attacker contact, preserves records, and seeks trusted support. Recovery of money is not guaranteed.

outcome.label: Takeover progressed; full recovery started
outcome.heading: You changed course and addressed every access path
outcome.explanation: The complete late response may limit further harm while still acknowledging the device, profile, payee, and transaction consequences.

warningSigns.sign: A later safe response does not erase the period of attacker control.

artifact.heading: Only part of the progressed takeover is secured
artifact.message: Some access is restored, but email, sessions, profile details, payees, or transaction status still need review.
artifact.transcript: The attacker progressed through the phone number into bank access. A password change or one removed device is not enough to address every recovery path. The learner can still contact the real bank and carrier with the full timeline.

outcome.label: Takeover progressed; recovery incomplete
outcome.heading: Important access paths remain open
outcome.explanation: Partial action helps, but the earlier code, device, payee, and transfer consequences require a coordinated response.

warningSigns.sign: The restored phone signal can hide unresolved bank and email access.

artifact.heading: The connected accounts are under review
artifact.message: You used trusted channels to coordinate the carrier, bank, and email response.
artifact.transcript: The learner reports the unauthorized number transfer, bank changes, pending payment, and possible email exposure to the legitimate providers. Each provider will determine its available recovery steps. A pending transfer may or may not be stopped, so the scenario does not guarantee recovery.

outcome.label: Coordinated recovery
outcome.heading: You secured the full account chain
outcome.explanation: Independent contact, complete disclosure, and review of every connected access route provide the strongest response.

artifact.heading: Part of the takeover was addressed
artifact.message: The bank alert received attention, but carrier or email access may still support another reset.
artifact.transcript: The learner takes a useful step with the bank but leaves parts of the connected security chain unfinished. Contact the legitimate carrier and email provider through trusted channels, document the number transfer, review recovery methods, and terminate unknown sessions.

outcome.label: Partial recovery
outcome.heading: More access routes need review
outcome.explanation: Securing one account helps, but the compromised phone number or email may still reopen it.

artifact.heading: The account takeover remains active
artifact.message: The phone signal returned, but bank sessions, profile changes, payees, email access, or money movement may still be unauthorized.
artifact.transcript: The visible service outage has ended, but connected accounts remain exposed. This can happen to anyone. Use a trusted device to contact the carrier and bank immediately, tell them the complete timeline, secure email and recovery methods, preserve records, and follow their guidance. Recovery is not guaranteed.

outcome.label: Takeover unresolved
outcome.heading: Restored service was not complete recovery
outcome.explanation: Prompt, coordinated action can still reduce additional harm even when unauthorized access or money movement has already occurred.
